en: The sampaguita, our national flower, releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract hawkmoths for pollination.
The Philippine eagle uses its shaggy crown of dark feathers to shed heavy rainwater in its mountain habitat.
Narra, the national tree, drops its leaves during the dry season to conserve water and survive tropical droughts.
Ifugao farmers build stone-walled rice terraces following mountain contours to prevent soil erosion and capture natural spring water.
During the Pahiyas Festival, Lucban locals dye rice flour into kiping wafers that dry and harden under the sun.
Jose Rizal crossbred local orchids in Dapitan, producing new varieties like Dendrobium rizalianum to study plant heredity.
The national gem, the South Sea pearl, forms inside the gold-lipped pearl oyster found in the Sulu Sea.
Mindoro Mangyans carve Ambahan poetry onto bamboo tubes because bamboo's high silica content resists rot and preserves the writing.
Bohol's Chocolate Hills turn brown during the dry season because the sun bakes the grass covering the limestone mounds.
Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator that uses hot water bottles to keep newborns warm in rural clinics.
Ancient Filipinos carved Baybayin script onto bamboo tubes because bamboo's tough, silica-rich outer layer protects the etched writing from decay.
The Philippine Constitution guarantees all citizens the right to a balanced and healthful ecology in harmony with nature.
